passage:
Subject: Would you be my Friday check-in?

Dear Kalyani,

For two months I have been checking in about my portfolio project with a friend from the design team. It was warm and I loved it, but every week ended with "no worries, next week". Nothing moved. I think I need someone who will ask straight. You are senior in our studio, and when you reviewed my slides last month you were kind and also clear about what was missing, so may I ask you? Here is my idea for the format: ten minutes on Friday, and three lines from me beforehand: what I did, what is next, what is stuck. You ask about those three, nothing else. If it stops being honest, we say so and stop. Would that work for you?

Pooja

qa.q: What three lines will Pooja send beforehand?
qa.a: Pooja will send three lines: what I did, what is next, what is stuck.

qa.q: What could Pooja and Kalyani do if the Friday format starts to feel like a formality?
qa.a: They could change the questions or look at a piece of finished work together, so that the check-in stays honest.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel on receiving the request?
qa.a: Kalyani may feel flattered and a little responsible, and may appreciate that the format is short and clear.

passage: You asked what finally fixed my study plan for the bar exam. I'm Ankita. My first accountability partner was my best friend from college. Every Sunday she'd ask, "How was your week?" and I'd say, "Busy," and she'd say, "Same, don't stress." Six weeks, nothing done. So I changed partners. I asked Ritu, a senior associate at my firm, who is kind but doesn't let things slide. We agreed on a format: every Friday, a five-line message. What I finished. What I didn't. Why. What's next. One thing I need. Ritu replies with one question, never a lecture. The first Friday I had to write "didn't" three times. It was embarrassing. But by the fourth week, the "didn't" line was empty.

qa.q: What five lines go in the Friday message?
qa.a: What I finished, what I didn't, why, what's next, and one thing I need.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel the first Friday with Ritu?
qa.a: Ankita felt embarrassed writing "didn't" three times, but the honesty was the point.

qa.q: Which approach suits Ankita better than the first partner, and why?
qa.a: A kind but firm partner with a fixed format, because it asks for facts and next steps instead of letting "busy" end the conversation.

qa.q: How might Ritu see the Friday messages?
qa.a: Ritu seems to see it as a light but steady job: one question, never a lecture, which keeps it honest without pressure.

passage: I'm Farida, and I sit across from Pema at the design studio. For two months I watched her "check in" with a friend on the phone every Monday, laughing, saying things like "Oh, I'll catch up." Her portfolio for the scholarship didn't move. Then one Monday she walked over to our senior designer's desk with a printed sheet. I overheard a little: "Three questions, every Thursday. What did I do? What's next? Where am I stuck?" The senior agreed on ten minutes, no more. After that, every Thursday at four, Pema sat at that desk with her sheet. Sometimes she came back looking frustrated. But the portfolio pages started appearing on her pinboard, one or two a week. I can't say what changed inside her. The pinboard changed, though.
